prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Beginning, The, And

outputs.L1:
Beginning to dangle beneath  
the wind that blows from the undermined wood,  
I feel the great pulley grind,  
the thread I cling to lengthen  
and let me soar and spin down into marble,  
hooked and weightlessly happy,  
where the squared sun shines back equally  
from all four sides—out of stone  
and years of dazzling labor—

to land at last among men  
who cut, with power saws, a Parian whiteness  
and, chewing slow tobacco,  
their eyebrows like frost,  
shunt house-sized blocks, lash them to cables,  
and send them heavenward:  
into small-town banks,  
into the columns and statues of government buildings,  
but mostly graves.

I mount my monument and rise,  
slowly and spinningly, from the white-gloved men  
toward the hewn sky,  
out of the basement of light,  
sadly lifted through time’s blinding layers  
on, perhaps, my tombstone,

in which the original shape  
Michelangelo believed was in every rock upon earth  
is heavily stirring,  
surprised to be an angel,  
to be awakened in North Georgia by the ponderous play  
of men with ten-ton blocks—

but no more surprised than I  
to feel sadness fall away, as though I myself  
were rising from stone,  
held by a thread in midair:  
badly cut, local-looking, and wholly uninspired—  
not a masterwork,  
or even worth seeing at all,  
but the spirit of this place just the same,  
felt here as joy.
outputs.L2:
I begin to hang below the current sweeping out of the hollowed quarry. Above me, an enormous wheel groans; the line supporting me unspools, lowering me in wide, turning arcs into the marble pit. Suspended from a hook, I am buoyant with delight. The sun, made angular by the quarry, strikes back with equal force from its four stone walls—surfaces exposed through years of brilliant toil.

At last I descend among the workers. With power saws they slice the Parian-white rock. They chew tobacco deliberately, their brows dusted pale as ice, while they maneuver blocks as large as houses, bind them with cables, and hoist them toward the world above. The marble will become pillars and figures for civic buildings and banks in little towns, though most of it is destined for burial markers.

Then I climb onto my own memorial and begin to ascend, slowly revolving, guided by men wearing white gloves. I move toward a sky carved open above the quarry, leaving its luminous depths and passing mournfully through the glaring strata of time. Perhaps I am being carried upon my own gravestone. Inside it, the hidden form that Michelangelo thought inhabited every earthly rock starts to move with effort, astonished to discover that it is an angel—roused in northern Georgia by the heavy choreography of men handling ten-ton slabs.

Yet its amazement is no greater than mine as sorrow slips away. I seem to be emerging from the rock myself, hanging in open air by a single cord: crudely fashioned, provincial in appearance, wholly lacking inspiration—not a masterpiece, not even something anyone would consider worth viewing. Still, I embody the soul of this place, and here that soul is experienced as happiness.
outputs.L3:
The speaker imagines hanging from a pulley and being lowered deep into a marble quarry. Suspended above the excavation, the speaker feels almost weightless, experiencing exhilaration rather than fear. Below, quarry workers labor to cut enormous blocks of white marble from the earth, move them across the site, and hoist them toward the surface. These heavy stones will eventually be shaped into the imposing facades of banks and government buildings, public statues, and, most significantly, gravestones.

The speaker then imagines rising from the quarry on a block of marble destined to become a tombstone. The ascent seems like a journey through layers of geological and human time, while the form hidden within the stone gradually awakens. Yet the figure that emerges is not an ideal masterpiece of the kind Michelangelo might have uncovered. Instead, the marble is carved into an imperfect, locally crafted angel—modest, flawed, and ordinary.

Although the finished monument lacks artistic greatness, it still possesses deep emotional power. The spirit of the quarry, the workers, and the surrounding place gives the angel meaning beyond its craftsmanship. Through this connection, the speaker’s sorrow is transformed into a sense of wonder and joy.
outputs.L4:
I imagine descending into a marble quarry in the mountains of North Georgia, moving deeper into the pale earth where stone is cut from stone. The walls bear the scars of drills and saws; dust hangs in the air, and enormous blocks wait to be lifted into daylight. From here, the marble will travel outward into the world. Some pieces will become courthouse columns, statues, or monuments. Others will be polished into headstones and placed above the dead, their smooth surfaces engraved with names, dates, and brief declarations of love.

As I descend, I think of Michelangelo’s belief that every block of stone already contains its true form. The sculptor’s task, he said, is not to invent but to release—to remove whatever conceals the figure waiting inside. Yet the marble around me does not seem to promise only masterpieces. It contains flawed surfaces, rough angels, unfinished bodies, and forms no practiced hand has perfected. Its beauty lies partly in those irregularities: the visible cuts, the broken edges, the evidence of pressure and labor.

In my imagination, I become one of those figures. I rise from the quarry like an angel carved by an uncertain hand, my wings uneven and my face still bearing the marks of the chisel. I am not graceful by the standards of great art. I am too rough, too human, too incomplete. But as I climb toward the light, the sadness I carried below begins to fall away like marble dust.

What remains is joy—not the flawless joy of a finished masterpiece, but something sturdier and more honest. The quarry’s spirit is imperfect, local, and alive. It teaches me that transformation does not depend on becoming immaculate. We may emerge scarred, awkward, or unfinished and still rise. Transcendence is possible even for the crudely carved; perhaps it is our roughness that proves we have truly been shaped.
outputs.L5:
**Beginning, The, And**

Every story starts with a **beginning**—a quiet moment when possibility becomes real. **The** first step may feel uncertain, but it gives direction to everything that follows. Then comes **and**, a small word that connects one moment to the next: courage and doubt, failure and growth, endings and new beginnings.

Together, these words remind us that life is not a single event. It is a continuing story, always opening another door, adding another chapter, and inviting us to begin again.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about descending into a North Georgia marble quarry and experiencing a spiritual transformation while watching workers lift enormous blocks of stone.
counterfactuals.output:
We went down before the heat,  
past kudzu loosening its green grip  
on the red shoulders of the road,  
past pines holding their dark counsel  
over North Georgia.

The quarry opened without warning—  
a white wound in the earth,  
terraced and immense,  
its flooded depths the blue  
of something remembered in prayer.

Each step lower  
cooled the blood.

Marble walls rose around us,  
veined with smoke, with rose,  
with the slow handwriting of pressure.  
Here, time had not passed—  
it had gathered,  
mineral by mineral,  
into weight.

Below, the workers moved  
in helmets bright as votive flames.  
Their saws entered the mountain  
with a thin metallic hymn.  
Cables tightened.  
Chains trembled.

Then an enormous block lifted—  
not quickly,  
not cleanly,  
but with the grave reluctance  
of a buried truth.

It hung above the quarry floor,  
white and shadowed,  
large enough to become  
a courthouse, a headstone,  
a saint’s calm shoulder.

The men raised their hands,  
calling to one another  
through dust and thunder,  
guiding the stone  
as if guiding a soul  
unaccustomed to air.

And I, who had carried  
my own unshaped heaviness  
for years,  
felt something in me answer—

not release, exactly,  
but the first taut pull  
of an unseen cable,  
the first deep shift  
after long burial.

Dust settled on my arms  
like ash, like blessing.

When we climbed back out,  
the afternoon burned  
on every cut face of marble.  
The pines stood where they had stood.  
The red road waited.

But the world had altered  
by one impossible lifting:

what I had called weight  
was also substance,  
what I had called darkness  
had veins of light,

and even the earth,  
split open,  
was giving up  
something luminous.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a long, surreal poem in the style of James Dickey, using imagery of pulleys, cables, marble monuments, tombstones, laborers, and an imperfect angel rising from stone.
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write in James Dickey’s exact style, but I can offer an original poem with muscular, Southern-gothic imagery, surreal transformations, physical danger, and metaphysical intensity.

## **The Quarry’s Imperfect Angel**

At noon the quarry opened its white mouth  
and the men descended by cable,  
each wearing the small black sun  
of his shadow under him.

Pulleys turned in the wooden towers,  
complaining in voices of old women  
who had buried their wedding rings  
with husbands returned from the war.

The foreman lifted one hand.

Above him, the crane’s iron neck  
leaned over the pit,  
and a block of marble rose  
with the patience of a moon  
dragged out of the earth  
before its proper hour.

No one spoke.

The laborers had learned  
that stone was listening.

They stood with their hammers  
resting against their thighs,  
their shirts salted white,  
their faces grained with dust  
until each man seemed already carved  
for a monument no nation would raise.

All morning they had cut tombstones:

BELOVED MOTHER,  
FAITHFUL SON,  
A CHILD CALLED HOME—

the words shallow at first,  
then deepened by chisels,  
each letter becoming a room  
into which the dead might move.

Beyond the quarry, wheat fields trembled.  
Telephone wires crossed the heat.  
A hawk hung by invisible tackle  
over a pasture burnt yellow,  
its wings not beating,  
its black cable fastened somewhere  
past sight.

Then the marble block turned.

It turned slowly in the sling,  
white and enormous,  
giving back the sun  
as if the sun were a coin  
the earth had buried in its mouth.

A crack traveled through it.

The men heard the sound  
inside their teeth.

Not thunder.  
Not breaking.

Something more like a door  
remembering it had once been a tree.

The foreman shouted.

The pulleys seized.  
The cables tightened to a single note  
so high the living could scarcely hear it,  
though every tombstone in the yard  
leaned toward the quarry  
as though called by name.

And from the crack  
a shoulder appeared.

Not flesh.

Not yet.

A shoulder of rough stone,  
scarred by the drill,  
with one wing folded against it  
like a crushed ladder.

The men dropped their tools.

The hammers struck the ground  
and lay there shining,  
small stunned animals.

The figure rose by inches  
from the divided marble,  
not lifted by crane or cable  
but drawing the block upward with it,  
wearing its prison  
as a swimmer wears water.

First the head—

unfinished, one eye open,  
the other only a blunt hollow  
where darkness had set its thumb.

Then the mouth—

crooked, chipped,  
one lip beautiful,  
the other still fused  
to the silence of the quarry.

Then the hands—

five fingers on the right,  
three on the left,  
and from the broken palm  
a vein of iron glittering  
like blood unwilling to be red.

The imperfect angel stood  
on the suspended stone.

Its wings were unequal.

One spread broad and terrible,  
feathered in chisel marks,  
each feather sharp enough  
to sign a man’s name in granite.

The other ended at the elbow  
of heaven.

Dust fell from it  
in luminous sheets.

The laborers covered their faces,  
but through their fingers they saw  
the angel bend over them  
with the grave curiosity  
of something born too late  
to believe in birth.

Who made me? it asked.

Its voice moved through the cables,  
through the crane’s gears,  
through the lunch pails  
and the water barrel,  
through the rings on the hands  
of men who had forgotten  
the softness of their wives.

No one answered.

The sculptor was dead.

He had been dead a hundred years,  
buried under a monument  
cut from this same vein of marble,  
his name eroded,  
his stone angel perfect  
except for the rain  
slowly removing its face.

Who made me?  
the quarry asked through the angel.

A laborer named Amos stepped forward.

He was thin as a crowbar,  
with blue scars in his palms  
and a cough he kept folded  
in a red handkerchief.

“We did,” he said,  
though he had never touched  
that buried figure,  
though his father had worked coal  
and his father’s father  
had drowned in a river  
trying to save a mule.

The angel looked at him  
with its one completed eye.

Then why, it asked,  
did you leave me unfinished?

At this the men laughed—

not because it was funny  
but because the day was too bright,  
the stone too white,  
the question too much like a mirror  
lowered among them.

They laughed until the pulleys shook.

They laughed until the marble monuments  
beyond the yard began giving up  
their carved dates.

Numbers slipped from the stones  
and crawled like pale insects  
into the weeds.

The dead, relieved of chronology,  
rolled over underground.

Mothers became daughters.  
Old soldiers became boys.  
A drowned child grew backward  
into the dark warmth  
before water.

The angel stepped from the block  
onto the air.

The air sagged.

Invisible rigging took its weight.

Every cloud tightened like a fist  
around some celestial rope,  
and the whole sky lowered  
one blue inch.

The laborers felt it.

Their knees bent.

Their spines remembered  
the ancient load:  
mountains, masters, wages, sons,  
the names of the dead cut straight  
while the lives of the living  
wandered crookedly.

The angel raised its broken hand.

A cable snapped.

It flew upward wildly,  
lashing the tower,  
slicing through a beam  
thick as a church pew.

The crane tilted.

The marble block swung out  
over the men,  
a white pendulum  
counting the final second.

They ran.

All but Amos.

He stood beneath the stone  
looking up  
as if waiting for an answer  
to descend with full weight.

The angel moved.

Its sound wing beat once.

The quarry filled with night.

Its broken wing beat once.

Night shattered into feathers of light.

The angel caught the block  
against its chest,  
and where stone struck stone  
a wound opened—

not red,

but filled with grass,  
rain, horseflies,  
the smell of hot tin roofs,  
the cries of children  
leaping from rope swings  
into brown rivers.

From the wound poured  
all that marble had refused:

the sweat of nameless cutters,  
the bent backs of quarrymen,  
the lungs slowly whitening,  
the fingers lost to blades,  
the women washing dust  
from collars at midnight,  
the graves bought by the week.

The angel staggered.

Its single eye widened.

So this is flesh, it said.

And Amos, still beneath it,  
reached up with one scarred hand  
and touched the rough ankle.

“No,” he told it.  
“This is work.”

For a moment  
the earth released everything.

Tombstones rose from the cemetery  
on roots of cable.

Marble generals climbed down  
from their horses.

Judges abandoned their pedestals,  
leaving bronze robes  
standing empty in the squares.

Stone saints cracked open  
and flocks of blackbirds  
poured from their ribs.

Across the country  
monuments turned their faces  
away from victory  
and toward the laborers  
washing at pumps,  
sleeping beside furnaces,  
eating in the shade  
of machines that could kill them.

The imperfect angel saw them all.

It saw the woman  
whose hands packed cotton  
until her fingerprints wore smooth.

It saw the boy  
carrying bricks up a ladder  
that rose through clouds  
and ended under the boot  
of a marble king.

It saw men underground  
pulling darkness into carts.

It saw cables stretched  
from every human shoulder  
to an unseen weight.

Then the angel began to climb.

Not gracefully.

Its full wing heaved.  
Its broken wing clawed the air.  
It rose crookedly,  
turning, falling, rising again,  
each failure carrying it higher.

The pulleys screamed.

The cables, freed of machinery,  
unwound themselves  
and followed like serpents,  
like black veins drawn  
from the earth’s arm.

One cable wrapped the angel’s waist.  
Another bound its sound wing.  
A third entered the wound  
in its chest and came out  
streaming sparks.

Still it rose.

The men returned  
to the quarry’s edge.

Dust covered their hair.  
Blood brightened one man’s ear.  
Someone was praying.  
Someone else cursed God  
with such tenderness  
it became another kind of prayer.

Higher went the angel,  
dragging the crane’s shadow  
over the wheat fields,  
over barns and graveyards,  
over courthouses whose columns  
had never lifted anything.

At the height of the hawk  
it stopped.

Its unfinished face  
turned toward the sun.

The sun entered  
the hollow of its missing eye.

For one impossible second  
the angel saw perfectly—

not with symmetry,  
not with mercy,

but with the broken vision  
of all things made by hands  
that tremble, tire, bleed,  
and return at dawn.

Then it opened its crooked mouth.

No hymn came.

No trumpet.

Only the quarry whistle  
blasting the hour to resume work.

The sound crossed the fields.

The dead heard it  
and sat upright in their graves.

The monuments heard it  
and became ordinary stone.

The laborers heard it  
and looked at one another,  
each face imperfect,  
each body unfinished,  
each life still trapped  
in some white block  
the world intended to sell.

Amos picked up his hammer.

Above him the angel struggled  
against the cables,  
rising, sinking, rising—

never free,

never falling,

its one great wing  
beating the stone dust  
into weather,

its broken wing  
making, with every useless stroke,  
a small new piece of heaven.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a first-person poem in which the speaker dangles over a marble quarry, imagines traveling through the stone’s journey into banks, government buildings, and graves, and ultimately finds unexpected joy.
counterfactuals.output:
I hang where the quarry has opened the mountain,  
one boot skidding on powdered light,  
my hands clenched around a rusted cable,  
the white abyss breathing below.

In that depth, stone waits in bright rooms—  
veined thunder, buried milk—  
and I imagine going with it:

lowered by crane, split clean from darkness,  
lashed to a truck that crawls the switchbacks,  
carried past olives and sleeping roofs  
to the mouths of cities.

I enter a bank as a polished floor.  
Coins cross me all day like cold rain.  
I rise as columns around a courthouse,  
holding up laws no mountain ever needed.  
I become steps to a government hall,  
worn shallow by promises and shoes.

Then farther—quietly—I travel  
under the chisel’s patient alphabet.  
I stand in graveyards as angels,  
as dates, as names the weather softens,  
my pale hands folded above strangers  
who have finished falling.

Still dangling, I see all my futures:  
vault, pillar, monument, bone-white door—  
and laugh.

For a goat has appeared on the ledge,  
calm as a small god, chewing thyme.  
It looks at me, unimpressed,  
then leaps across the gap I fear.

The cable holds. The sun spills everywhere.  
Dust turns golden in my open mouth.  
I am not stone, not yet, not ever—  
I am the ridiculous weight of being alive,  
swinging over emptiness,  
unable to stop shining.
